s3.q: In Treisman's attenuation model, what happens at the first stage, where incoming stimuli are checked?
o: Stimuli are analysed fully for their meaning; relevant signals pass on to short-term memory and all the others are blocked
Stimuli are checked at a low level for features such as loudness and pitch; matching ones pass on, others pass on weakened
Stimuli are held in short-term memory until the listener decides which one of them deserves a response
Stimuli are checked only for personal importance; the listener's own name is let through and everything else is stopped there
s3.spot: 'What happens at the first stage' of a model = describe what is checked (physical features or meaning) and what happens to the rest (blocked or weakened).
s3.why: In Treisman's model, stimuli are first analysed at a low level for target properties like loudness and pitch, for example when listening for your partner's voice in a noisy bar. Signals that match pass on; those that do not are passed on in weakened (attenuated) form. Only in the next step is meaning analysed, which is why a meaningful word can still break into awareness.

s3.q: In Madden et al.'s (2002) visual search study, which brain areas were active during the most difficult search (conjunction search) in both younger and older adults?
o: The dorsal and ventral visual pathways and the prefrontal cortex
Only the right occipital cortex, and only in the younger adults
Only extra regions outside the visual pathways, recruited to compensate
Only the prefrontal cortex, with no visual areas involved at all
s3.spot: A brain-imaging finding + 'in both groups' = recall what the age groups shared, not where they differed.
s3.why: Conjunction search activated the dorsal and ventral visual pathways as well as the prefrontal cortex in both age groups, with about the same prefrontal and superior parietal activation. Older adults showed less right occipital activation, and they did not recruit regions outside the visual pathways to compensate.

s3.q:
Baggage screeners know they must look for weapons, search every bag for them, and still miss some of the rare weapons that appear. Judge these statements.
I. This is inattentional blindness, because the weapon is fully visible on the screen.
II. Missing a target you are searching for is stronger evidence for a real capacity limit than classic inattentional blindness.
o: Only statement I is true
Only statement II is true
Both statements are true
Neither of the two statements is true
s3.spot: I/II about a search task = first check the defining feature of inattentional blindness (unexpected), then ask what a miss despite searching shows.
s3.why: Statement I is false: inattentional blindness requires that the object is unexpected, and the weapon is exactly what screeners are looking for. Such misses point to other mechanisms, such as the low-prevalence effect (with rare targets people stop searching too early). Statement II is true: classic inattentional blindness can be explained away with 'you did not know to look', but here people know, search, and still miss.

s3.q: In research on inattentional blindness, what is meant by a person's attentional set?
o: The total amount of working memory capacity a person has available for the task at hand
The collection of objects a person has already seen and stored in memory
The features a person is attending to, such as the colour of the team being counted
The part of the visual field in which a person's eyes can see sharply
s3.spot: A technical term + 'what is meant by' = a definition; think of what you are tuned to look for.
s3.why: The attentional set is what you are tuned to look for, such as white shirts when you count the white team's passes. Unexpected objects that match the set are noticed far more often (Most et al., 2001), which is why noticing depends on what you attend to, not purely on where you look. Working memory capacity and visual sharpness are different concepts.

s3.q: Which criticism applies to Deutsch and Deutsch's late-selection model but NOT to Broadbent's early-filter model?
o: It cannot explain why anyone notices their own name in the unattended ear
It is wasteful: every message is fully analysed for meaning, then most of it is thrown away
It cannot explain why listeners notice a male voice changing into a female voice in the ignored ear
It assumes that the unattended message is weakened rather than blocked
s3.spot: 'Applies to X but NOT to Y' = think of each model's typical weakness: an early filter lets too little through, a late filter processes too much.
s3.why: In late selection, all input, attended or not, is analysed for physical properties and meaning before the filter, which seems wasteful when most of it is then discarded. Broadbent's early filter has the opposite problem: it cannot explain why anyone notices their own name, because meaning is never analysed. Weakening the message is Treisman's idea, and both models can explain noticing a voice change.

s3.q: In Sternberg's Figure 4.9, Treisman's model is drawn as a flow from input to response: sensory register, attenuation control, a limited-capacity stage, perceptual processes, short-term memory. Unlike in Broadbent's version, the unattended stream is drawn continuing past the control stage. What does this continuation represent?
o: A weakened version of the unattended message that still travels on toward meaning analysis
The part of the unattended message that is blocked completely at the sensory register
Only the listener's own name, which is the one part of the unattended message that is let through
A copy of the attended message that is stored in short-term memory for later use
s3.spot: A flow diagram + 'what does this line represent' = compare it with the other model's diagram: does the ignored stream stop or go on?
s3.why: In Treisman's diagram the filter works like a volume knob: the unattended stream is turned down, not off, so both streams reach the limited-capacity stage and continue toward perceptual processing. In Broadbent's diagram, by contrast, the unattended stream stops at the filter. The difference between stopping and attenuating is the whole difference between the two models.

s3.q: A delivery company wants to reduce accidents in which drivers fail to notice cyclists. Which measure fits the advice in Simons' module best?
o: Give every driver a hands-free kit, so that phone calls no longer interfere with watching the road
Train drivers to notice everything around them, so that inattentional blindness disappears
Hire only drivers with a high working memory capacity, because they reliably notice the unexpected
Lock the phone away while driving, instead of relying on drivers' willpower to resist it
s3.spot: A practical measure + 'fits the advice' = recall what Simons says can and cannot be done about inattentional blindness.
s3.why: Simons' advice is to avoid distractions when an unexpected event could be catastrophic, and to be proactive: put the phone out of reach rather than trusting yourself to resist it. Hands-free calling does not help, because the limit lies in central attention, not in the hands. Noticing everything is impossible (and would not be desirable), and the evidence on working memory capacity is mixed.

s3.q: A psychologist asks children to sort picture cards by colour. After a while she announces a new rule: sort the same cards by shape. Several children keep sorting by colour for a few cards, even though they understood the new rule. Which explanation from the task-switching research fits best?
o: Mixing cost: keeping two rule sets ready slows down every single trial in the mixed block of trials
Mere presence effect: the cards themselves draw attention away from the task
Task-set inertia: the previous rule set is still active and interferes with the new one
Preparation effect: the children had too much time to prepare for the new rule
s3.spot: An old rule that keeps intruding after a switch = ask which account says the previous task set lingers.
s3.why: After a rule change, the previous task set (sort by colour) is still active and interferes with the new one: task-set inertia (Allport, Styles & Hsieh, 1994), in effect proactive interference at the level of rules. The mixing cost compares repetition trials in a mixed block with a single-task block, and more preparation time reduces switch costs rather than causing them.
